extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, regulators, scholars, and students interested in financial regulation and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and chapter-level criteria for designing financial regulation that enhances system stability and protects consumers, emphasizing market-based approaches rather than centralized command-and-control rules. Covers capital rules, failure resolution, securities and derivatives regulation, consumer finance, innovation (cryptocurrency/fintech), and regulatory process improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure resilience of the financial system
rubrics_metrics.description: Design a regulatory framework that ensures the resilience of the financial system so it can continue to serve consumers, investors, and small businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation should enable the system to handle shocks and avoid crises that disrupt credit access and savings; this is a high-level goal underlying the book's chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support economic growth and individual prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation should support economic growth and individual prosperity by allowing financial markets to create opportunities for consumers, investors, and small businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rules by their impact on capital availability, investment opportunities, and households' ability to save for the future; avoid rules that unduly hinder economic activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address too-big-to-fail and too-small-to-borrow problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory design must confront systemic issues like institutions that are too big to fail and gaps that leave small firms or borrowers without access to credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should reduce moral hazard from bailouts and ensure access to credit for small borrowers; consider whether new rules mitigate or exacerbate these problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reimagine regulatory framework from the ground up
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than layering new rules on top of existing ones after crises, pursue comprehensive rethinking of the regulatory architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ad hoc additions that create an unwieldy framework; favor coherent redesign that addresses root causes and systemic incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor market discipline and oversight over centralized, top-down regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches should rely less on centralized, top-down regulations and more on market discipline and oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider mechanisms that harness market signals and private incentives (e.g., loss-absorbing capital, contractual risk-sharing) instead of prescriptive mandates where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate risk sharing through market mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation should facilitate risk sharing across market participants to spread and manage financial risk efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether rules enable markets to allocate risk (e.g., via securities, derivatives, intermediation) rather than artificially concentrating or socializing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiently provide access to capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory policy should enable efficient provision of capital to firms and households.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether regulatory requirements impede capital formation, increase cost of capital, or create barriers that hinder economic growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable households to save for the future
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation should protect and enhance households' ability to save and invest for retirement and other long-term goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess consumer-protection measures and market structures for their effects on saving opportunities and long-term financial security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-Based Capital Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt capital requirements tied to the riskiness of assets to ensure loss absorption by institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how risk weighting, measurement, and calibration affect resilience; weigh complexity versus effectiveness and whether rules create perverse incentives or regulatory arbitrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simpler, higher capital requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider simpler and higher minimum capital requirements as an alternative design for loss absorption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simpler rules may reduce complexity and gaming; higher capital increases buffers but may affect lending and cost of capital—balance simplicity, sufficiency, and economic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore alternative mechanisms to the FDIC model for protecting depositors and managing bank failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate different loss-absorption and depositor-protection approaches (e.g., market-based substitutes) and their incentives, moral hazard, and fiscal implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credible failure-resolution regimes (Title II / bail-ins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design credible frameworks for addressing firm failures, including contemplation of Title II (orderly liquidation authority), bail-ins, and other resolution tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess credibility of resolution mechanisms to avoid bailouts; consider legal, operational, and market effects of bail-ins versus government intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use market mechanisms to manage proprietary algorithmic trading
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply market-based approaches to address risks posed by proprietary algorithmic trading instead of heavy-handed prescriptive regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider market incentives, exchange rules, or architectural changes that mitigate harmful outcomes while preserving innovation and liquidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broker-dealer regulation reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsider how US broker-dealer regulation is structured and enforced to better align with market functions and investor protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine statutory responsibilities, supervision models, and whether existing rules achieve intended protections without unduly restricting market intermediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsider Dodd-Frank swaps trading regulatory framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Reevaluate the swaps trading rules established under Dodd-Frank for effectiveness and unintended consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether swaps trading regulations improve transparency and reduce systemic risk or instead impede risk-sharing and liquidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rethink the swaps clearing mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: Question the mandated central clearing of swaps as the default risk-management approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits of central clearing (mutualization of default risk) against costs (concentration of risk, procyclicality, margin demands) and consider alternatives or refinements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate exchanges' roles as regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the historical and potential role of exchanges acting as regulators within securities and derivatives markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether exchanges can effectively police markets, balance conflicts of interest, and foster competition compared with government regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offering and disclosure reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform securities offering and disclosure regimes to improve investor information and market functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on meaningful disclosures that reduce information asymmetries while avoiding excessive compliance burdens that impede capital formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-reinforcing versus market-replacing consumer finance regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose between consumer finance rules that reinforce market functioning and those that replace market outcomes with regulatory substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor interventions that correct market failures and preserve market discipline rather than substituting regulatory dictates that can reduce consumer choice or access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful examination of interest-rate cap policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Scrutinize arguments for interest-rate caps and their likely market effects on access to credit and borrower welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate empirical and theoretical consequences (e.g., credit rationing, shadow markets) before adopting caps intended to protect consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulating Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies on principled grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the appropriate grounds and principles for regulating Bitcoin and similar digital assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether regulation should target functions (payments, securities, commodities), consumer protection, market integrity, or systemic risk, and tailor rules accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial technology (fintech) regulation that balances innovation and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Design fintech regulation that enables innovation while providing necessary safeguards for consumers and markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider light-touch, technology-neutral rules, sandbox approaches, or targeted safeguards that avoid stifling beneficial financial innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of federal corporate law centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate proposals that would centralize corporate law at the federal level (the 'specter of a federal corporate law') and whether to end it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze implications for state corporate governance, regulatory competition, and businesses' legal environments before advocating federalization or its removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) for financial regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether and how regulatory impact analysis of financial regulations is possible and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use RIA to quantify benefits, costs, and trade-offs of rules; acknowledge methodological challenges in measuring systemic and long-term effects and strive for transparent, evidence-based analyses.
